title: Chapter 178 – The Third Wave
html:
[The Valley Wall, Sections One and Two – Lan Wen]

Lan Wen has been blind for sixty-one years, and in all that time the dark has never frightened her.

It is the one thing she has over the sighted. They cannot bear it. She has watched a hundred strong men go white when a lamp blew out, and a thousand more go quiet in a cellar, listening for the sound of their own fear. She has never understood it. The dark is only the absence of a certain kind of news. There are other kinds. She hears the breath of a man and knows his lie. She feels the heat of a body through a stone wall. She reads the world as a deep slow pattern of heat and pressure, a weather of living things, and she has long since stopped missing the sun.

Tonight, for the first time, she is afraid of the dark.

She stands on the parapet of section two with her hand on the cold stone and her face turned to the south, and she feels the Wall hum beneath her palm like a plucked wire. All along the two-mile line the lamps burn: a thousand of them, in braziers and lanterns and rows of clay cups, lit at dawn from the Garden's carts. The Sect pupils have strung them on cords between the buttresses. The Garden guards have hung them from spear-points. The drums beat in the courtyards. It is the loudest, brightest, strangest battlefield she has ever stood on, and all of it is happening in a place she cannot see.

She feels the tide. That is the dreadful part. She has felt it for four days, a slow pale pressure against the south face of the Wall, like a sea leaning on a dyke. But tonight it has changed.

"Sera," she says.

"Captain." The girl at her elbow is twenty-two, a lean sharp-faced Garden scout with a bandaged hand. She has been Lan Wen's eyes since the first night. She does not describe things. She only tells her where to point. "I'm here."

"Tell me what the lamps are doing."

"They're... fine, Captain. They're burning. Why?"

"Because the tide has stopped trying to climb." Lan Wen's blind face tilts. "Do you hear it? That is not the sound of a siege. A siege is a thing that pushes. This is a thing that waits."

Sera is quiet. Out beyond the light, where the killing ground ends and the dark begins, there is no sound at all.

"It's thinking," she says at last, in a small voice.

"Yes."

"Beasts don't think."

"No. They don't." Lan Wen straightens. She lifts her hand off the stone. "Something is thinking for them."

* * *

She has the council in the Gate tower at the second hour of the night, because someone has to say it aloud.

They are all there: Han, gaunt and sleepless, with a fresh bandage on her forehead; Lu Fei, hunched over his Weights; the Elders of the Sect, a dozen men and women in dusty gray, who have all aged ten years in a week. Jian is in the corner on a stool with a blanket round his shoulders and a cup of Bell's black bitter tea. He has not spoken. He looks like a man who has been hollowed with a spoon. But his eyes, which are not blind, follow her across the room.

"The tide is not what it was," says Lan Wen. "It has divided."

"Explain," says Han.

"There were three kinds, at the start. The crawlers, which are stupid and quick. The Gnashers, which are stupid and strong. And what I will call the Riders, the beasts with a master, whom I felt on the second night and could not name. I have been listening to them. I believe I understand them now." She lowers herself onto a bench, with Sera's help. "A Rider is not one creature. It is two. A beast, and a thing that sits upon its back. The beast has a body. The rider has a mind. And the mind..." She frowns. "It does not belong to the rider. It is lent."

"Lent by whom?"

"I do not know." The white eyes close. "There is a thread. I can feel it when a Rider is near me, a fine bright line of will running back into the dark. The line goes to the south, along the valley, a long way. It is very strong. And it is aware of me." She opens her eyes. "I think that when I listen to the Riders, it listens back."

Nobody speaks.

"How many?" asks Han, at last.

"Forty. Fifty. They are gathering at the foot of the Wall, in the dark between the lamps. They are choosing a point." Lan Wen's voice is very even. "They will go for the place where the Wall is thinnest."

"Section nine," says Lu Fei at once. "But Elder Gu's keystone..."

"Holds. Yes. I felt it too. It is a very bright thing, that array. I could not have missed it." A faint, wintry smile. "They know it is strong. They will not go there. They will go where the lamps are fewest and the pupils are tired. They will go for the corner."

"The corner?" says Han.

"Sections one and two. Mine." Lan Wen lifts her face. "The place where the Garden's guards stand beside your pupils. The oldest joint. The one where the two lines are stitched together."

A long silence.

"Then we reinforce it," says Han.

"With what?"

"I can give you three hundred pupils."

"You cannot, Head, and you know it." Lan Wen speaks quite gently. "If you pull pupils from the center, you open the center. The Third Wave will not strike where we are strong. It will strike where we have moved." She folds her hands. "I have two hundred guards. I have been counting them since dawn. I would like to keep them where they are."

"And if the Riders break through?"

"They will not."

"You cannot promise that."

"No," says Lan Wen. "But I can stand in the way."

Across the room, Jian has put down his cup. He is looking at her very steadily, with his thin gray face, and for a moment she thinks he will speak. He does not. He only bows his head.

It is an Elder's bow. It is the bow of a man who has said the same words to others and meant them.

* * *

Between the council and the line, she lets herself stop for one breath at the foot of the tower stair, and remembers.

She remembers the day she came to the Garden. She is sixteen, and blind from a childhood fever, and her uncle has sold the last of the family's goats to pay the road. She stands in the yard of the Lin clan's gate-house with a stick in her hand and a bundle on her back, and she can hear the people around her deciding what to do with her. Nobody is cruel. That is the worst of it. They are only kind in the way people are kind to a stray: a bowl of soup, a corner by the stove, a gentle voice saying poor thing.

Then a woman's voice, brisk and low, says: "Can she hold a spear?"

"She's blind, Mistress."

"I didn't ask if she could see it. I asked if she could hold it." A pause. A rough, warm hand takes hers and closes it round a shaft of ash-wood. "Well, girl?"

She remembers the weight of it. She remembers the answer she gave, which was not brave at all, only stubborn. Show me where to point it.

That was Zhao, thirty years younger, new to the Seat and short of guards. It was the only time in fifty-four years that anyone gave her a task before they gave her pity. She has never forgotten which came first.

She breathes out. She gathers her cloak. She climbs the stair.

* * *

She walks her line before the fight, as she has every night.

It takes an hour, because the line is long and she stops at every post. Two hundred guards, in quilted gowns and leather caps, spread across two sections of a Wall that was not built for them. She knows them all by voice. She knows the new ones by their breathing, the old ones by the creak of their knees. She stops at each. She says a name, and a small true thing, and goes on.

"Dun. Your wife had the baby."

"Yes, Captain." The man gives a startled laugh. "How did you..."

"You hum when you think of it. A girl?"

"A girl."

"Then you have something to come home to. Keep your head down."

"Mara. The cough is better."

"Much better, Captain."

"Don't lie. Hold the spear in the left hand tonight and rest the right."

She goes along the whole line like that, with Sera at her shoulder. Some of them are young enough to be her grandchildren. Most are farmers' sons and orchard daughters who took the guard's pay for the winter bread. They have never been asked to be brave. Tonight they are being asked, and every one of them stands up straighter when she passes.

At the end of the line, at the corner joint where section one meets two, Jian is waiting.

He has come out alone. He has refused the stretcher, the guard, the stool. He leans against the parapet with the staff between his knees and the blanket slipping off his shoulder, and she can hear the faint wet catch in his breath.

"You should be in the tower."

"I should be many places." His voice is dry. "You told Han the Riders would come here."

"I did."

"And you will stand in the way."

"I will."

He is silent for a moment. A lamp sputters somewhere to the right.

"I am going to ask you not to," he says.

She turns her white eyes on him. "Why?"

"Because you are the best captain the Garden has ever had, and the best I have ever worked with, and I have fifteen weeks to spend and I do not want to spend them without you." He says it plainly, the way a man reads a figure from a ledger. "That is selfish. I know it is. I said it so that you would know."

Lan Wen is quiet for a long time. Then, slowly, she puts out her hand and lays it flat against his chest, above the heart, as she once did for a dying friend, years ago, who wanted to be told the truth. The heartbeat under her palm is quick and shallow and uneven. It is a clock run down to its last turns.

"I am seventy," she says. "I have buried everyone I ever loved. I have been standing at the edge of a great dark thing for most of my life and calling it duty. Tonight I would like to stand in front of it. Not behind." She takes her hand away. "It is not a sacrifice, Jian. It is a preference."

"I understand."

"Then do me one kindness."

"Anything."

"Do not follow me when I go. You will want to. Your whole life you have followed people into the dark, because you cannot bear to be the one left standing." The faint smile. "Stay. Be the one left standing. It is also a duty."

He bows. He does not answer. She did not expect him to.

* * *

The Riders come at the fourth hour, and they come in a line.

She feels them long before the sentries sound the horn: a cold, deliberate, well-ordered pressure, spread across a hundred paces of the killing ground, advancing without hurry. No scrabble. No rush. Fifty beasts on six jointed legs, each with a pale figure upright on its shoulders, walking out of the black into the glow of the lamps.

"They're not afraid of the light," says Sera, and her voice shakes.

"No. The riders see for them. Their master does not need the dark." Lan Wen draws her sword. It is a plain steel blade, old, nicked, without ornament, and she has carried it for fifty years. "Pass the word. Spears in the first rank. Crossbows behind. Hold until I say. Hold until they are at the foot of the Wall."

"Captain..."

"Hold."

They hold. She stands in the center of section two with her hand on the parapet, listening to the footfalls. A hundred paces. Seventy. The rhythm of it is hypnotic, a great slow hoofbeat of bone on stone. She counts it under her breath. Sixty. Fifty.

At thirty paces, the nearest Rider lifts its head and speaks.

It is a thin, sweet, almost gentle voice, with no sound in it that a living throat could make. It comes across the killing ground like cold water poured into a cup.

"Captain Lan Wen," it says.

The guards stiffen.

"We have been listening to you for four days. You have a very fine mind. It is a pity to waste it." A pause. "Open the gate."

"No," says Lan Wen.

"We do not wish to harm you. We wish to speak with the keeper. The old man in the gray cloak, who came back from under the tree." A faint, patient sadness. "He has something that belongs to us. We would like it returned."

She does not turn her head. She does not let her face move. But she feels, on the far side of the parapet, behind her, the faint sudden warmth of Jian rising to his feet.

"There is no one here by that name," she says.

"You are not a good liar, Captain. You are very honest. It is why we like you." The voice almost smiles. "Give him to us, and we will turn aside. We will go around your Wall. We will not trouble you again."

"And the rest of the valley?"

"Is not your concern."

She says nothing for a moment. The wind is cold on her face. Beyond the voice, far away, down the long bright thread of will that she can feel with every sense she possesses, something vast and silent has turned its attention upon her. It does not feel evil. It feels like a person at the edge of a very deep pool, patiently waiting for a fish.

"I have served the Lin clan for fifty-four years," she says. Her voice is steady. "I was blind when I came to them, and nobody cared. They gave me a post, and a spear, and a place at the table. They never asked what I could not do." She lifts the sword. "You may tell your master that I decline."

"That is regrettable," says the Rider.

It lunges.

* * *

It is the longest night of her life, and she remembers very little of it.

She remembers the sound. A roar, a slam, the impact of fifty bodies against the stone. She remembers Sera's hand clamped on her sleeve, hauling her left, right, down, away. She remembers the heat of the lamps and the stench of blood. She remembers the guards. Their voices, calling the time. Hold! Hold! Brace! The ugly bright crack of crossbows. The thump of spears into flesh. The Garden's two hundred, who have never fought as a line in their lives, fighting as one body, because she told them to.

She fights. She is not a young woman and the sword is not light. But she needs no eyes to cut, and no light to kill, and she knows where every Rider stands by the cold bright thread of will that runs from its back. She follows the threads. She cuts them. Twice she takes a rider off its beast with one stroke, and the thing screams, a thin human sound, and drops, and the beast beneath it halts as if its strings had been cut.

That is the secret, she thinks. The riders are only the knots. Cut the knot, and the beast is a beast.

She tells Sera. Sera shouts it down the line. The guards take it up, and the crossbows turn from the beasts to their riders, and one by one the pale figures topple. The line of Riders thins. The roar of the assault begins, for the first time, to falter.

And then the thread tightens.

She feels it like a hook behind her breastbone. A cold steel tug, from the dark, a long way south, and in the same instant every surviving rider on the killing ground goes rigid and turns its head toward her.

"Captain Lan Wen," says the voice. It is a different voice now. It is deeper, and quieter, and it comes from all fifty mouths at once. "You are in the way."

She sets her feet.

The Rider nearest her launches itself at the parapet in a single enormous leap, and she meets it with the sword. The blade goes in under the chin and out through the back of the skull. The thing falls across her, heavy, thrashing, and its needle mouth snaps shut an inch from her throat. She drives the sword in again. The jaws go slack.

She rolls clear. She is gasping. Something has gone wrong in her side, a hot wet wrongness, and when she puts her hand there it comes away dripping.

"Captain!" Sera is on her knees. "Captain, you're hit, you're..."

"It is nothing."

"It's not nothing, it's..."

"Sera." Lan Wen catches her wrist. "Listen to me. The Riders have stopped. Tell me they have stopped."

The girl looks up. Lan Wen feels her do it, feels the sudden shift of heat as her head turns, and the long shaky breath that follows.

"They've stopped," Sera whispers. "They're just... standing there. All of them. Looking at you."

"Yes." Lan Wen smiles. "I thought so."

She has understood, at last, what the thread wants. It does not want the Wall. It does not want the gate. It wants her: her mind, her white eyes, the strange trained sense that listens back. She is a bright small lamp in the dark, and the Alpha at the end of the line has been trying all night to reach her.

Then let it, she thinks.

She lets go of the thread. She does the thing she has never done in sixty-one years of reading the weather of living things. She opens herself to it entirely, and follows the line back.

* * *

The world goes white, and then it goes wide.

She sees. Not as the sighted see. She sees as the thing itself sees, through a hundred eyes at once, through fifty riders on fifty beasts, through the dim crawling dark of the valley floor. She sees the Wall from below, a great pale bar, banded with gold. She sees the lamps, each one a little scream of light. She sees herself, tiny and fragile on a parapet, with a sword in her hand.

And she sees, at the far end of the line, the thing that is looking back.

It is vast. It is not a beast. It is an arrangement, a pattern of living tissue the size of a hill, buried in the earth, a hundred thousand fine pale fibers threaded through the valley's rock like the roots of a tree. In its center, deep, deep, so deep that she can only feel the shape of it, there is a slow dim pulse. A heart. A great cold slow heart, beating once in a hundred of her own.

Oh, she thinks. There you are.

The Alpha knows she is there. It does not move. It does not speak. It only turns its enormous attention on her, and she feels the weight of it settle on her mind like the sea settling on a stone.

You can see, it says.

It is not a voice. It is a feeling, vast and slow and strangely tender.

You can see me. No one has seen me in a thousand years.

Why are you here? she asks, with the last of her breath.

I was set to keep, it says. I was set to keep the door shut. And someone opened it, from the other side, and I forgot what I was keeping.

And she understands. Not all of it. A fragment, a splinter, enough to carry. She sees the shape of the thing's hunger and the shape of its grief, and she sees the place in its great slow heart where a single bright wire has been driven in, like a nail through a hand.

It is hurt, she thinks. It is not a monster. It is hurt.

She tries to say it. She tries to put the knowledge into words, to carry it back up the thread to the one who needs to hear. But she is very tired. Her side is wet and cold. Somewhere above her, a long way off, a girl's voice is calling her name.

Tell Jian, she says, to the Alpha, to the dark, to anyone. Tell him where the nail is.

And the thread snaps.

* * *

She comes back to a night full of lamps.

She is lying on the parapet with her head in Sera's lap. The battle is over. She can tell by the silence, the thin ringing hush that follows, and by the smell of smoke and oil. The Riders are gone. They fell back, Sera says, all at once, as if a rope had been cut, and the killing ground is empty. The Wall holds. The corner holds. The two hundred stand.

"Eleven dead," says Sera, and she is crying. "Eleven. We held. Captain, we held. You did it."

"Good." The word is very faint. "That is good."

"Don't talk. The healer's coming. Bell's pills, there's a boy running..."

"Sera." Lan Wen lifts a hand. It trembles. It finds the girl's cheek, wet and warm, and rests there. "Listen. There is a thing I must give you. Not the sword. The sword is nothing. A name."

"Captain..."

"You will be Captain of the Garden guard. I have written it in the Roll. Pei An has the paper." The white eyes are open, blind and serene. "Do not let Zhao argue. She will say you are too young. You are. That is how it is done."

"I can't."

"You can. You have been doing it for four days." Lan Wen smiles. "You told me where to point."

A step on the stone. A shadow falls across her face, thin and slow, and she feels the faint worn warmth of a man with fifteen weeks in his chest. She does not need eyes. She knows him by the sound of his breath.

"Jian," she says.

"I'm here."

"There is a nail." She finds his sleeve. Her grip is surprisingly strong. "In the Alpha's heart. A bright wire, driven in from outside. It is not a master. It is a prisoner. Someone has been using it, and it does not want to be used." She coughs. "Find the nail."

"I will."

"And Jian."

"Yes."

"The kettle." Her voice is almost a whisper. "Tell Qinghe I always meant to say. Her tea was never as bad as I told her."

He laughs. It is a short, wet, shattered sound, and she feels the tears fall on her wrist.

"I'll tell her."

"Good." Lan Wen lets her head fall back against the girl's knee. The lamps burn gold on her blind face. For the first time in sixty-one years, she can see the light, and it is exactly as everyone said. "It is very bright. I did not know it would be so bright."

She is still smiling when Han comes up the stairs, and kneels, and bows to the ground.
